query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiphase high-entropy alloys, controlled thermal annealing that induces a moderate degree of grain-boundary segregation and the in-situ formation of metastable secondary phases will enhance toughness retention via transformation toughening mechanisms, whereas excessive annealing leads to over-segregation and nanoclustering at grain boundaries that cause decohesion and a loss of toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast (or as-sintered) multiphase high-entropy alloy (e.g., a Cantor-type alloy) with a relatively homogeneous grain-boundary chemistry and without engineered secondary precipitates.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the annealing temperature and dwell time to control the degree of grain-boundary segregation and the formation of secondary phases.
generation.conditions: Testing under demanding engineering conditions including high strain-rate deformation and a moderate-to-high service temperature regime where microstructural stability and transformation effects are active.
generation.structural_mediator: The chemical composition at the grain boundaries and the spatial distribution and size of in-situ precipitates.
generation.mechanism: A moderate level of annealing promotes the nucleation of metastable secondary phases along grain boundaries which, under applied loads, can undergo a stress-induced transformation that enhances toughness (transformation toughening). However, excessive annealing increases the extent of grain-boundary segregation leading to nanocluster formation that weakens intergranular cohesion and initiates decohesion or cavitation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an as-cast baseline, samples annealed at an optimal temperature/time window will show improved toughness (higher fracture strain and energy absorption) due to effective transformation toughening, while samples subjected to higher annealing severity will display a reduction in toughness due to grain-boundary embrittlement.
generation.baseline: The as-cast or as-sintered HEA with minimal long-range grain-boundary chemical segregation and without engineered precipitate formation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for HEAs with multiphase or heterogeneous microstructures under mechanical loading conditions relevant to demanding engineering applications (e.g., high strain rate, fluctuating temperature) and may not apply to single-phase HEAs or systems where additional environmental factors (e.g., oxidation) dominate the failure behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold values for annealing temperature and time that delineate the beneficial versus detrimental regimes are system dependent and require further calibration. Additionally, the transformation kinetics of the secondary phases under load are not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple identical HEA samples and subject them to a series of thermal annealing treatments varying temperature and dwell time over a calibrated range. Use high-resolution microscopy (TEM, STEM-EDS) to quantify grain-boundary segregation and precipitate formation. Perform mechanical testing (e.g., fracture toughness tests, high strain-rate compression/tensile tests) to measure toughness.
measurements: Grain-boundary composition and precipitate size/distribution (via TEM, STEM-EDS)
Load–displacement behavior under high strain-rate conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no systematic correlation is observed between the degree of controlled grain-boundary modifications (segregation and precipitate formation) and the measured toughness (i.e., if samples showing moderate annealing do not exhibit enhanced toughness relative to both the as-cast baseline and excessively annealed samples), then the proposed mechanism of transformation toughening versus decohesion via over-segregation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) of the Cantor type (CoCrFeMnNi) are widely recognized as model systems for studying the relationships between composition, microstructure, and functional performance. In this study, atomized Cantor alloy powders were consolidated using spark plasma sintering (SPS) under systematically varied process parameters (temperature and dwell time). The densification behavior, microstructural evolution, and mechanical response were investigated using Archimedes’ density measurements, Vickers hardness testing, compression tests, scanning electron microscopy, and EDS mapping. The results reveal a non-linear relationship between sintering temperature and densification, with maximum relative densities obtained at 1050 °C and 1100 °C for short dwell times. Despite the ultrafast nature of SPS, grain growth was observed, particularly at elevated temperatures and extended dwell times, challenging the assumption that SPS inherently limits grain coarsening. All sintered samples retained a single-phase FCC structure with homogeneous elemental distribution, and no phase segregation or secondary precipitates were detected. During the tensile test process at intermediate temperatures in the air, intermetallic phases were not yet formed in coarse-grained Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni HEAs, owing to a short testing time (a few minutes). In addition, the above-mentioned oxide and hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms can be ruled out because these alloys show good resistance to oxidation at intermediate temperatures and hydrogen embrittlement at relatively low hydrogen concentrations (, ). These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.

frame.system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) developed for demanding engineering applications, starting from a microstructurally complex state with multiphase or heterogeneous microstructures.
frame.goal: To develop and test a mechanistic hypothesis that explains the retention or loss of toughness in HEAs by linking controlled microstructural modifications to observed toughness behavior.
frame.limitation: An incomplete understanding of the intrinsic mechanisms governing toughness retention or degradation, particularly under varying processing or environmental conditions.

frame.regime: Experiments designed to simulate demanding engineering conditions (e.g., high strain-rate, varying temperatures, cyclic loading) where microstructural stability and deformation mechanisms are stressed.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have suggested that factors like grain boundary decohesion, phase transformation toughening, or local chemical ordering may impact toughness. However, they did not systematically correlate controlled microstructural modifications (e.g., controlled annealing or alloying adjustments) with toughness retention across a defined range of conditions, leaving the mechanistic picture incomplete.

decision.trend: Early studies first observed that toughness loss in single‐phase HEAs can be linked to local chemical inhomogeneities – specifically, nanoclustering at grain boundaries that undermines cohesion (PMC6897545). Later work in high-entropy carbides demonstrated that deliberately introduced, metastable in-situ particles can transform under stress and yield enhanced toughness (PMC10504279). In both cases, the focus was on correlating particular microstructural modifications (either unintentional segregation or deliberately engineered precipitates) with changes in ductility or toughness. However, the controlled, systematic adjustment of the microstructure to test a mechanistic link between a specific modification and toughness retention under demanding conditions has not yet been fully realized.
decision.unsolved: While grain-boundary chemistry, nano-precipitate formation, and transformation toughening have been implicated, it remains unsolved how a controlled change in microstructural state in multiphase, complex HEAs directly governs toughness retention or loss. In particular, the quantitative role of controlled phase segregation at grain boundaries or the formation of transformable secondary phases in determining toughness boundaries under high strain-rate, varying temperature, and cyclic loading conditions is still unverified.
decision.lever: systematically vary thermal annealing conditions (temperature and time) to induce controlled grain-boundary segregation and in-situ precipitation of secondary phases that are capable of transformation under load
decision.why: This approach builds on prior evidence where uncontrolled nanoclustering (leading to decohesion) and induced metastable particles (yielding transformation toughening) affected toughness. By using a controlled annealing process, the experiment can reveal how the deliberate adjustment of grain boundary chemistry and secondary phase distribution correlates with changes in toughness relative to an as-cast baseline, defines the valid operating boundaries (under high strain-rate and temperature variations), and allows for falsification if no systematic toughness retention or loss is observed.
